making.intro: From finding the stone to the final polish, making a sculpture involves choices that are difficult to see in the finished piece. The process varies by artist and material, but every stage requires experience, care and physical work.

sections.heading: Finding and moving the right block
sections.body: The work can begin long before the artist picks up a chisel. Zimbabwean sculptors may travel to a quarry or work with stone suppliers to find material with the right size, colour and structure. They inspect the block for weaknesses and natural markings, knowing that a hidden fracture could prevent a particular design. A large block can weigh substantially more than the finished work and may require several people to move. For some artists, sourcing and transporting the stone takes most of a day. These decisions and costs come before carving begins.
sections.caption: A rough block at the workshop. The quarry itself is not shown.

sections.heading: Working out what the stone will allow
sections.body: The sculptor studies the block and decides where the main forms, openings and supporting sections can be. Some artists mark an outline first; others develop the composition as they carve. A loop, for example, cannot simply be drawn onto the surface. The artist must work out how to remove stone from its centre while keeping the surrounding structure intact. Figures present different challenges: a small change to the angle of a head or the distance between two bodies can alter the meaning of the work. This judgment develops over years of practice.
sections.caption: The artist works beside a substantial block of stone.

sections.heading: Removing stone without losing the sculpture
sections.body: The rough form is often cut with a hammer and chisel, breaking away material one strike at a time. Depending on the stone and the artist, drills, grinders or other tools may also be used. The work demands strength, concentration and control. Unlike clay, a section taken off cannot simply be put back. One poorly placed blow may crack a narrow connection or force a change to the entire piece. As the rough block takes shape, the artist must continually judge what can be removed and what has to remain.
sections.caption: Hammer-and-chisel work during carving.

sections.heading: The slow work of curves, details and balance
sections.body: Once the main form is visible, the work often becomes slower. Smaller tools refine the curves, recesses, facial features and edges. Narrow bridges of stone must be strong enough to hold their own weight, even when the finished sculpture appears almost weightless. The sculptor works around the piece repeatedly, checking proportion and the view from different sides. Each curve is also a physical surface that has to be reached and finished. What appears effortless in the gallery may have required many careful corrections in the workshop.
sections.caption: The artist refines a recessed area with a hand tool.

sections.heading: Sanding, polishing and revealing the stone
sections.body: The carving may be recognizable long before it is finished. Tool marks are removed with abrasives, moving through progressively finer grades until selected surfaces become smooth. Curved interiors and small corners can be especially time-consuming. For some serpentine stones, artists heat the surface, apply a clear wax and buff it to deepen the appearance of the natural colour. Others retain rough or unpolished areas beside the finished planes. The exact method depends on the stone and artist. By the end, the surface can look completely different from the dusty block with which the sculptor began.
sections.caption: Surface texture during carving, before final polishing.

making.closing: The value of a finished sculpture is not measured by the amount of stone left in it. It also reflects an artist's originality, years of experience, difficult decisions, quality of execution and the individual character of the work.

house.vision: Zimbabwean stone sculpture is contemporary art made by individual artists, each with their own interests and way of working. We want the people who encounter these pieces to know more than how they look. Understanding the artist and the work behind the finished surface changes how you see it.
house.founders: Bradley and Milton founded House of Mabwe to introduce these sculptures to a wider audience. We believe the work deserves the same attention given to contemporary sculpture from anywhere in the world, with proper credit for the person who created it.
house.approach: We bring together carefully selected works and present them with photographs, available 3D views and useful information about each sculpture. We want buyers to understand the material, the craftsmanship and the individual artist, while keeping the artwork itself at the centre of the experience.

rhythm.intro: Long curves, loops and openings give these pieces their movement. Each one relies on carefully placed connections that keep the form intact.

elemental.intro: These works draw attention to the stone itself: its veins, changing colours, rough edges and areas the artist has chosen to polish.

presence.intro: A small change in the angle of a brow, cheek or profile can give a carved face an entirely different expression.

kinship.intro: Paired and grouped figures show how much can be communicated through posture, proximity and the spaces between bodies.

wild-grace.intro: From recognizable animals to more abstract forms, these sculptures capture character through line, balance and proportion.

zsa-013.editorialShort: The sculptor has taken the movement of fire and translated it into a form that can stand still. The two sides rise from the same base, pull apart and bend toward one another without closing the space between them. It suggests the energy of something that keeps changing, even when its source remains the same. Much of the work lies in what has been removed: the opening gives a heavy block of stone its sense of movement.

closerLook.heading: The central opening
closerLook.copy: The two sides rise from a heavy base and narrow as they curve toward each other. The sculptor has carved through the centre while leaving enough stone for the upper form to remain supported. This open space defines the sculpture from every angle.

zsa-009.editorialShort: This sculpture considers the relationship between two forms that belong together without touching. A rounded centre is held inside a larger looping shape, suggesting a planet following its path or two people moving within each other's lives. The sculptor has used a continuous curve to give the eye somewhere to travel, then placed the sphere where that movement seems to gather. The idea is about connection, but also the space each part needs to remain itself.

closerLook.heading: The loop around the centre
closerLook.copy: From the right side, look at the depth of the carved loop and the space left around the rounded centre. The thickness of the surrounding stone changes as the curve turns. Those connections keep the two forms visually balanced while holding the work together.

zsa-025.editorialShort: Two paths cross, separate and meet again in this abstract sculpture. The idea is familiar from life: people and decisions can move in different directions and still return to a shared point. Rather than illustrating a particular event, the sculptor builds that idea through interlocking curves and several open spaces. The pale natural markings pass through the turns in the stone, adding variation that no drawing or repeated mould could exactly reproduce.

closerLook.heading: Where the curves cross
closerLook.copy: The left-side photograph shows how the curving sections sit at different depths. Look at the gaps between them and the narrow places where one part of the composition joins another. These spaces are carved out of the original block, not assembled from separate pieces.

zsa-029.editorialShort: A new leaf slowly opening is one way to understand this work. The stone starts from a narrower lower form and expands into curves that turn back on themselves. It can also be read as a person finding room to grow after a period of restraint. The sculptor has avoided a literal plant or figure, concentrating instead on the change from tightness to openness. That gradual transition is what gives the piece its character.

closerLook.heading: The widening upper form
closerLook.copy: Seen from the right, the upper curves project beyond the stone beneath them. Their width and direction change along the length of the piece. The sculptor has kept enough material at each turn to support the wider sections without making the form appear heavy.

zsa-021.editorialShort: Several forms reach upward from a shared base, like hands lifted in greeting, hope or an appeal for help. They do not rise at identical angles, and that difference makes the gesture feel collective rather than rehearsed. The work offers no answer about what they are reaching for. Instead, the sculptor gives shape to a human impulse almost everyone recognizes: wanting something beyond the place where we stand.

closerLook.heading: The separate reaching forms
closerLook.copy: Each slender upper section extends in a slightly different direction. The sculptor has cut between them while keeping their connection to the base secure. Viewed from an angle, the spacing between the forms becomes easier to appreciate.

zsa-028.editorialShort: The red stone and crossing curves suggest the force of water moving around obstacles. A current rarely follows a straight line; it changes course but continues forward. The sculptor has turned that movement into a series of openings and overlapping shapes, allowing the natural red and darker mineral areas to remain visible. What makes this piece interesting is the combination of an imagined movement and the very real markings already present in the block.

closerLook.heading: The colour within the curves
closerLook.copy: In the left-side view, follow the red and darker markings as they pass around the carved bends. These variations belong to the stone itself. The polished faces expose them differently from the narrower edges, so the colour changes with the angle of the sculpture.

zsa-017.editorialShort: A rounded form sits within a more angular outer structure. It can be read as a person or idea held inside something protective, with enough room to remain independent. That tension between shelter and freedom is central to the composition. The sculptor has made the frame firm and geometric, while the form inside it is softer. The open space separating them keeps the sculpture from becoming a closed, solid block.

closerLook.heading: The space around the centre
closerLook.copy: The rounded centre is surrounded by a more angular frame. Carving the gap between them leaves a narrow amount of material at the points where the forms meet. The contrast between curved and straight surfaces is especially clear from the side.

zsa-031.editorialShort: This abstract work can be read as a protective presence rather than a portrait of a spirit. Its green and rust-coloured stone surrounds an irregular opening, combining worked curves with areas that retain more of the original rock. The suggestion is that protection does not always come from something visible or easily named. Here, the sculptor uses the material's natural variation to keep that idea grounded in stone rather than turning it into a literal figure.

closerLook.heading: Natural stone beside polished form
closerLook.copy: The right-side view makes the changes in surface treatment easier to follow. Some areas retain an uneven texture while the neighbouring curves are more carefully finished. The rust and green mineral colours pass through both, showing how the artist worked with the material already in the block.

zsa-012.editorialShort: The sculptor leaves a rough section of stone beside a clearly shaped human face. One possible reading is that our identities are formed by the places and experiences we come from, even as we grow into something distinct. The portrait does not try to hide the original rock. Its unworked surface remains present next to the defined features, allowing the viewer to see the person and the material together.

closerLook.heading: The face and the original rock
closerLook.copy: Look at the transition between the defined facial profile and the rougher rust-coloured section beside it. From the left, the difference in depth and finish is particularly clear. The sculptor has refined one area and retained the irregular surface of the other.

zsa-001.editorialShort: This head is recognizable despite having very few conventional facial details. A circular opening gives the viewer a place to look through the stone rather than only at it. The sculpture suggests the experience of witnessing something: being present, looking carefully, and carrying away your own understanding. Instead of carving a detailed expression, the sculptor has made the empty space part of the face, leaving the interpretation open.

closerLook.heading: The opening through the face
closerLook.copy: The circular opening replaces detail that might otherwise have been carved onto the surface. It also changes how light passes through the work. From the side, the thickness of the stone surrounding the opening becomes visible.

zsa-026.editorialShort: The long face and strongly patterned upper section suggest a person whose position carries both recognition and responsibility. A crown or headdress can communicate status, but the sculpture gives equal importance to the calm expression below it. The sculptor has deliberately separated these two visual elements: detailed grooves above, restrained facial features beneath. The result feels less like a celebration of power than a portrait of someone expected to carry it well.

closerLook.heading: The shape of the crown
closerLook.copy: The right-side view shows how the grooved upper section rises beyond the flatter facial plane. Repeated cuts give it a distinct texture, while the face below remains comparatively smooth. The change in thickness is more visible in profile than from the front.

zsa-023.editorialShort: The face is built from rising points and angled planes rather than soft, rounded features. It suggests someone looking ahead while carrying the marks of difficult experience. The sculptor gives that idea an upright, forward-moving outline, with surfaces that catch the light differently as the work is turned. There is no elaborate expression to explain how the figure feels; the attitude comes from the position and proportions of the head.

closerLook.heading: A face built from angles
closerLook.copy: From the left, the planes of the forehead, nose and jaw can be followed as separate carved surfaces. Small changes in their direction alter the profile of the head. Those precise transitions, rather than fine facial ornament, give the sculpture its expression.

zsa-027.editorialShort: A composed face sits below a forehead that retains a much rougher surface. The contrast suggests a difference between what people show to the world and the thoughts or experiences they carry within. The sculptor has made the lower face calm and recognizable while refusing to smooth away the stone above it. The unfinished-looking area is not simply an absence of work; it gives the portrait another part of its story.

closerLook.heading: The rough forehead
closerLook.copy: In the right-side photograph, the rough pale forehead projects above the smoother facial surface. The boundary between them remains visible, along with the difference in texture. The sculptor has chosen not to polish those two areas into the same finish.

zsa-020.editorialShort: Two people lean toward one another until their bodies become one connected form. The work is about the ordinary act of giving and receiving support, not a dramatic scene. Their heads are close, and neither figure appears to stand entirely apart from the other. The sculptor has kept enough distinction for us to recognize two individuals while joining them through the stone. That balance gives the embrace its meaning.

closerLook.heading: How the figures support each other
closerLook.copy: The right-side view shows how the two bodies meet and where the artist has left openings between them. Their heads and shoulders remain distinct, but the lower forms stay connected. The gesture depends on those small changes in position rather than detailed facial expressions.

zsa-014.editorialShort: Two faces appear beneath a shared arrangement of carved grooves. They can be understood as people shaped by the same family, place or experience, yet still recognizably different from one another. The sculptor gives them separate profiles but connects them through the upper form, making their relationship visible without showing an embrace. It is a quiet study of what people share and what remains individual.

closerLook.heading: Two different profiles
closerLook.copy: The left-side image shows the depth of the profiles beneath the grooved upper section. Look at the different angles of the foreheads and faces. The repeated cuts above them visually connect the figures, while the outlines below keep them separate.

zsa-007.editorialShort: The figures are close enough to feel connected, but each retains a distinct shape and posture. That makes the work less about an idealized couple than about the effort of moving toward another person. The sculptor has left space between parts of the bodies while bringing the heads together, turning a simple gesture into the subject of the piece. The contrast between textured and smooth areas adds to their individuality.

closerLook.heading: The space between the bodies
closerLook.copy: From the right, the separation between the two slender bodies becomes easier to see. Their upper forms turn toward one another while the lower stone keeps the composition connected. The openings were carved out of one block and had to be shaped without weakening the piece.

zsa-010.editorialShort: Two faces move toward a kiss, caught at the point where the distance between them almost disappears. The sculptor has chosen a small, recognizable moment instead of a grand romantic scene. Their profiles tell us what is happening before any fine facial detail is needed. The open space around them matters as much as their contact, because it lets the viewer see both individuals and the closeness between them.

closerLook.heading: The meeting of two faces
closerLook.copy: The right-side photograph reveals the depth of the two profiles and the narrow space around them. Their noses, foreheads and chins establish the moment. The sculptor has kept the surrounding stone joined while separating enough material to make each face recognizable.

zsa-024.editorialShort: A group of figures is gathered within a rough oval shape, suggesting family or a community held together by shared experience. The people are not identical, and they do not need to be. The sculptor gives each figure enough definition to stand apart while using the surrounding stone to bring them into one composition. The outer edge feels more natural and less controlled, as if the group has been found within the rock itself.

closerLook.heading: The depth of the surrounding frame
closerLook.copy: The right-side view shows that the oval frame has real depth around the figures, rather than being a flat border. The outer stone is rougher than the carved forms inside it. That contrast helps separate the people from the rock that surrounds them.

zsa-005.editorialShort: Two long-beaked birds share one upright form, each looking in a slightly different direction. The work brings to mind the companionship that can exist without constant contact or attention. The sculptor has given each bird its own posture while keeping their bodies connected through the same stone. Their beaks and necks make the relationship immediately recognizable, even though the anatomy has been simplified.

closerLook.heading: The birds' different postures
closerLook.copy: In the left-side view, the long beaks and necks give the birds separate profiles. The small changes in the angle of each head prevent the composition from becoming symmetrical. Carving between those narrow forms requires more control than shaping the broader base.

zsa-006.editorialShort: A bird becomes almost entirely a curve in this sculpture. Its head and neck lead into a spiral, suggesting the circular movements seen in flight, nesting or the natural world. The sculptor has kept only enough of the animal to make it recognizable, letting the continuous turn carry the rest of the idea. It is an example of how an observed subject can become an abstract form without losing its character.

closerLook.heading: The carved spiral
closerLook.copy: Seen from the right, the inner opening of the spiral and the thickness of the surrounding curve become clearer. The sculptor has shaped the inside as carefully as the outside. The long neck leads into that turn, connecting the bird to the abstract form around it.

zsa-018.editorialShort: The animal lifts its head as though it has heard something beyond our view. The long ears and curved neck are enough to convey attention without showing a landscape or another creature. The sculpture turns listening into a physical posture. It also gives a familiar animal form a quiet dignity: for a moment, stillness is the most important action.

closerLook.heading: The lifted head and neck
closerLook.copy: The left profile makes the upward turn of the neck particularly clear. Its thickness changes as it supports the projecting head, and the long ears extend above the face. These are the main details the sculptor uses to give the animal its alert expression.

zsa-016.editorialShort: This work captures the suggestion of an animal or bird in the middle of movement, without trying to reproduce every detail of its body. The projecting sections read like a gesture caught between two positions. The sculptor has built the sense of motion through the outline and the direction of the forms, leaving viewers to complete the action in their imagination. It is a study of movement rather than a literal portrait of an animal.

closerLook.heading: The projecting forms
closerLook.copy: From the right side, the extensions stand apart from the compact centre of the sculpture. The openings and changing thicknesses make the silhouette feel active. The artist has kept those projecting forms connected to the main body while removing much of the stone around them.

hos-queen-mother.editorialShort: Queen Mother presents authority as something carried with composure. The wrapped headdress, earrings and layered necklaces establish the figure's status, but her expression is calm rather than commanding. The portrait can be read as a tribute to women whose influence comes from experience, care and responsibility within a family or community. Tinodashe Mangenda gives the face room to hold our attention, then uses the finely carved dress and jewellery to tell us more about who she is.

closerLook.heading: The headdress and jewellery
closerLook.copy: The right-side photograph shows how far the wrapped headdress extends beyond the face. Deep grooves separate its folds, while finer cuts define the earring, beads and necklace layers. Those details are carved from the same stone as the portrait, not attached afterwards.

hos-celebration.editorialShort: A seated musician plays a drum, recalling the gatherings where music brings people together. The figure could be starting a song, keeping a familiar rhythm or inviting others to join in; the sculpture leaves that moment open. The subject is deliberately ordinary, which is part of its appeal. The artist has brought the musician's hands, body and drum into one connected piece so the act of playing becomes the centre of the composition.

closerLook.heading: The musician and the drum
closerLook.copy: The right-side photograph shows the angle of the seated body in relation to the drum. The artist has carved the arms and hands around the instrument, keeping each part distinct while retaining the connections needed to support the whole sculpture.

hos-belonging.editorialShort: Four faces occupy a single open stone frame. None is quite like the others, but they share the same structure and space. The sculpture presents belonging as a relationship between individuals, not a demand that everyone look or think alike. Its simple arrangement allows different readings: a family, a circle of friends, or the experience of finding a community where one is accepted. The artist has made that shared connection part of the stone itself.

closerLook.heading: The carving behind the four faces
closerLook.copy: The rear photograph reveals the same four rounded forms and the open centre from the opposite side. Here, the thickness of the surrounding frame and the material supporting the individual heads are clearer. The sculptor had to leave those connections strong while opening the spaces between them.

hos-inner-beauty.editorialShort: An elongated face sits beside a more intricately patterned section of stone. The contrast invites a reading of beauty that goes beyond an elaborate outward appearance. The sculptor keeps the expression relatively simple and places the detail where it will reward a closer look. The portrait suggests a person whose character is not immediately announced, but gradually becomes apparent through small features and the care with which they are made.

closerLook.heading: The patterned surface beside the face
closerLook.copy: In the right-side photograph, the smoother facial profile meets a section of closely carved patterning. The difference in depth is easier to see at this angle. Individual cuts give the textured area its rhythm without changing the broad outline of the face.

hos-tall-attention.editorialShort: A tall figure bends toward a smaller one held close to the body. That single movement gives the sculpture its meaning: attention is shown through action, not through words. The difference in height might suggest a parent and child, a mentor and learner, or simply someone making space for another person. The sculptor has used the lean of the larger figure to make the smaller figure the centre of the encounter.

closerLook.heading: The two figures meeting
closerLook.copy: The detail photograph brings the upper figures closer, showing where the taller form bends toward the smaller one. The relationship depends on their different heights and the curve between them. The artist has left the gesture clear without adding a complicated scene around it.

hos-kissing-lovers.editorialShort: Two long faces meet in a kiss above an open centre. The sculptor has chosen a private, everyday gesture and made it the whole subject, without adding a setting or an elaborate story about the couple. Their hair and profiles form two distinct figures, but the point where they meet joins the composition together. The work can stand for romantic love, but also for the trust and familiarity that grow from being close to someone over time.

closerLook.heading: Where the profiles meet
closerLook.copy: From the right, the two elongated faces come together above the open centre. The carved lines of the hair run behind them and help distinguish the figures. The negative space below keeps the composition open while the upper stone remains connected.
